subject: ela
skillName: Write routinely for a range of tasks and audiences
description: Students learn to write routinely over both extended time frames (research, reflection, and revision that unfold over days) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or on-demand response) for a range of discipline-specific tasks, purposes, and audiences. Because this is a range-of-writing standard, items focus on the decisions a writer makes before and during writing rather than on grading a finished multi-paragraph essay. Given a short prompt, scenario, or stimulus embedded inside the item, students identify the purpose of a piece of writing (to inform, to persuade, to narrate, to explain), identify the intended audience and how that audience shapes tone and word choice, match a task to the time frame and process it calls for (a quick journal entry versus a researched report), choose the form or format that fits the task (letter, lab report, story, summary, argument), and recognize how purpose, audience, and task together shape the way a writer plans, drafts, and revises. They distinguish on-demand writing tasks from extended-process tasks and select the planning step, tone, or format that best fits a given discipline (a science observation, a history account, an English literature response). Every item embeds any prompt, scenario, or sample text it depends on inside the item itself, so the student needs nothing external. Items test these component decisions through identification, matching, and analysis rather than full essay production.
subSkills: Identify the purpose of a writing task (to inform, persuade, narrate, explain, or reflect) from a prompt or scenario
Identify the intended audience for a piece of writing and explain how the audience shapes tone, formality, and word choice
Distinguish writing tasks that call for an extended time frame and a multi-step process from tasks meant for a single shorter sitting
Match a writing task to the form or format that best fits it (letter, report, story, summary, argument, lab observation)
Recognize how purpose and audience together shape a writer's planning and revising choices
Match a writing task to the academic discipline and the kind of discipline-specific writing it requires (science, social studies, English)
Choose the appropriate first planning step for a task based on whether it is on-demand or extended
Adjust tone and register in a short sample so it fits a stated audience and purpose

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the purpose of the task
problemArchetypes.example: Read the short prompt embedded in the item: 'Write a piece convincing your principal to add a recycling program at school.' What is the main purpose of this writing? Options: to persuade; to entertain with a story; to explain a science process; to describe a vacation. Answer: to persuade, because the writer is trying to convince the principal to take an action.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the audience and its effect on tone
problemArchetypes.example: Read the prompt in the item: 'Write a thank-you note to your grandmother for a birthday gift.' Who is the audience, and how should that shape the writing? Options: a family member, so the tone is warm and personal; a teacher, so the tone is formal and academic; a scientist, so it uses technical terms; an unknown crowd, so it stays neutral. Answer: a family member, so the tone is warm and personal.

problemArchetypes.name: Sort the time frame the task requires
problemArchetypes.example: Read the two tasks in the item: (1) a quick five-minute journal entry about your weekend and (2) a researched report on a country, with sources, that is due in two weeks. Which task calls for an extended time frame with planning, research, and revision? Answer: the researched report, because it requires gathering sources and revising over many days, while the journal entry is a single short sitting.

problemArchetypes.name: Match the task to the right form or format
problemArchetypes.example: Read the task embedded in the item: 'Record what you observed during a plant-growth experiment in science class.' Which form best fits this task? Options: a lab report or observation log; a personal narrative; a persuasive letter; a poem. Answer: a lab report or observation log, because the task is to record factual observations from an experiment.

problemArchetypes.name: Match the task to the discipline-specific writing
problemArchetypes.example: Read the prompt in the item: 'Explain the causes that led to a historical event using dates and facts from your textbook.' Which discipline and writing type does this task belong to? Options: social studies, an informational explanation; science, a lab report; English, a short story; art, a caption. Answer: social studies, an informational explanation, because it asks for a fact-based account of historical causes.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the best planning step or revising move
problemArchetypes.example: Read the task in the item: a multi-day argument essay arguing whether students should have homework. What is the best first step before drafting? Options: list reasons and gather evidence to support a position; write the final copy in neat handwriting; pick a colorful font; copy a friend's opinion. Answer: list reasons and gather evidence, because an extended argument needs planning and support before drafting.

problemArchetypes.name: Adjust tone or word choice for the stated audience
problemArchetypes.example: Read the prompt in the item: a writer must email a school board member to request a new library book. Which sentence fits this audience and purpose best? Options: a polite, clear request with reasons; a slangy text-message style line; a one-word demand; an off-topic story. Answer: the polite, clear request with reasons, because a formal audience and a request purpose call for respectful, specific language.

Easy.description: A short prompt or scenario of roughly 20 to 50 words embedded in the item, naming a single clear writing task. The task is identify-level: name the obvious purpose, the obvious audience, or the obvious time frame of the task, where the clue words are explicit in the prompt. Only one component is tested and the correct answer is unmistakable.
constraints: Stimulus is a 20 to 50 word prompt or scenario included in the item
One component is tested (purpose, audience, time frame, or form) and it is signaled by explicit clue words
Identify-level task: name the purpose, audience, time frame, or matching form
Distractors are clearly wrong (a purpose that does not match the prompt, an audience absent from the scenario, a form that obviously does not fit)

Medium.description: A prompt, scenario, or short sample of roughly 50 to 110 words embedded in the item that involves more than one decision or a less obvious cue. The task is analyze-level: match a task to the right form, sort tasks by time frame, connect a purpose to the audience it implies, or judge how a stated audience should shape tone, where more than one option is plausible and the student must weigh fit. Light inference is required rather than reading a clue word directly.
constraints: Stimulus is a 50 to 110 word prompt, scenario, or short writing sample in the item
The cue is implied rather than stated word for word, or two components must be considered together
Analyze-level task: match task to form or discipline, sort by time frame, or connect purpose and audience
Distractors are plausible partial fits (a form that suits a related but different task, a tone close to but not right for the audience, a time frame that fits part of the task)

Hard.description: A richer scenario or short writing sample of roughly 110 to 180 words embedded in the item, with competing considerations or a more abstract judgment. The task is evaluate-level: decide which planning or revising choice best fits an extended versus on-demand task, judge which sample best matches a stated audience and purpose, choose the strongest reason a given form fits a discipline-specific task, or explain how purpose and audience together should shape a writer's choices. Requires inference about how task, purpose, audience, and time frame interact.
constraints: Stimulus is a 110 to 180 word scenario or sample included in the item
The judgment is abstract or multi-part (how purpose and audience jointly shape tone, why one form or planning step fits best among close options)
Evaluate-level task: select the best planning or revising move, the best-fitting sample, or the strongest explanation of fit among two or more on-topic options
Requires inference to weigh how time frame, purpose, audience, and discipline interact in the choice

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses the purpose of a writing task, treating any prompt about an opinion as a story or any informational task as persuasion
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels a persuasive task as 'to entertain' or an informational explanation as 'to persuade,' matching a surface topic word rather than what the writer is actually trying to do

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student ignores the audience and assumes every piece of writing uses the same neutral tone
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a tone or word choice that does not fit the named audience, such as a slangy line for a school board member or stiff formal language for a note to a friend

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student cannot tell an extended-process task from an on-demand task, judging time frame by topic instead of by the work the task requires
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls a quick journal entry an extended task or a multi-week researched report a single-sitting task, because the topic sounds big or small rather than because of the planning and revision it needs

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student matches a task to a form that does not fit its purpose, picking a familiar form over the right one
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a personal narrative or poem for a task that calls for a lab report or argument, selecting a form the student likes rather than the one the task requires

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assigns a task to the wrong discipline, missing the discipline-specific cues
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels a fact-and-date history account as a science lab report or an English short story, ignoring the kind of writing the discipline calls for

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student picks a late-stage or surface step as the first planning move for an extended task
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses 'write the final neat copy' or 'pick a font' as the first step instead of planning, gathering evidence, or outlining, treating presentation as planning

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats purpose and audience as separate and unrelated, changing one without adjusting the other
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a choice that fixes tone for the audience but abandons the purpose, or serves the purpose but uses a tone wrong for the audience, instead of balancing both

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes more formal or longer is always better, regardless of task and audience
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses the most formal or wordiest option even when the task calls for a short, casual, or to-the-point piece, mistaking length and formality for quality
